analysis.one_liner: Guarantees temp workers equal pay, wage transparency, safety training, and a ban on forced arbitration.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote: it sat across eight House committees from July 2020 until the Congress ended in January 2021, after sponsorship by one member and 11 Democratic cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set rules for the roughly three million Americans placed in jobs by temporary staffing agencies. It requires agencies and the companies using them to pay temp workers the same starting wage as permanent employees doing similar work, give workers written notice of each assignment and itemized pay statements, cover travel time between work sites, and stop charging workers for drug tests and background checks. It bans staffing agencies from forcing temp workers into arbitration, from blocking them with non-compete agreements, and from charging the host employer a fee when the temp is hired permanently after 60 days. It also adds safety training and hazard-analysis duties, creates a registration system for staffing agencies with Labor Department oversight, extends COVID-19 paid sick leave and family leave to workers at larger staffing agencies, and orders a Government Accountability Office study of how federal agencies use temp workers.
analysis.who_benefits: Temporary workers, who are disproportionately low-wage warehouse, manufacturing, clerical, and health-care support staff. Equal pay for substantially similar work, pay statements showing what the agency actually bills the host employer, coverage of travel time, and the right to decline strikebreaking assignments all raise what a temp takes home and how much control they have. Workers at larger staffing agencies also gain COVID-19 paid sick leave and family leave they were excluded from. The arbitration ban lets temp workers sue instead of being funneled into private arbitration they rarely win, and the retaliation presumption makes it easier to prove they were punished for complaining.

how_it_helps.text: Requires temp workers be paid no less than the average starting wage of permanent employees doing substantially similar work, with penalties for shortfalls
Requires 48-hour advance written notice of each assignment, including hours, wages, fees that will be deducted, and the rate the agency bills the host employer, plus itemized wage statements
Invalidates forced arbitration agreements for employment disputes between temp workers and staffing agencies or host employers
Bans non-compete agreements on temp workers and bans conversion fees charged to a host employer that hires a temp who worked 60 or more days
Requires safety training, a job hazard analysis before each assignment, and designation of which party provides protective equipment and workers' compensation
Extends COVID-19 emergency paid sick leave and FMLA coverage to temp workers at staffing agencies above the 500-employee threshold
Requires annual registration of staffing agencies with the Department of Labor, semiannual reporting, and a public list of registered agencies
Prohibits assigning temps to workplaces with strikes or lockouts without notice and the right to decline

analysis.who_pays: Temporary staffing agencies bear the largest cost: equal pay narrows the wage margin between what they charge host employers and what they pay workers, and they lose conversion fees, non-compete leverage, and forced arbitration as a shield. Host employers — manufacturers, warehouses, hospitals, and others that staff through agencies — face higher labor costs, pre-assignment hazard analyses, safety training duties, and recordkeeping. Smaller agencies would feel the compliance and registration burden most. Some of these costs would be passed into prices for the businesses that use temp labor.

drawbacks.text: Equal pay for substantially similar work narrows the gap between the bill rate and the temp's pay, which is how staffing agencies earn their margin; agencies could respond by raising prices, cutting placements, or shifting more work to independent contractors, and the bill explicitly defines temporary workers to include independent contractors

Banning conversion fees after 60 days removes a revenue source agencies rely on, which could push agencies to rotate workers off assignments before the 60-day mark to keep charging the fee, an outcome the bill does not directly prevent
Pre-assignment hazard analyses, training, and detailed recordkeeping within 48-hour deadlines are heavier compliance lifts for small agencies and small host employers than for large ones
Requiring host employers to verify agency registration each year adds a contracting step for every business that uses temp labor

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For temp workers the upside is direct and substantial: same work, same starting pay, knowing what the agency is charging for them, and a day in court instead of forced arbitration. The main honest tradeoff is that staffing agencies profit from the spread between bill rate and wages, and squeezing that spread could mean fewer placements or higher prices for clients — costs that fall partly on small businesses. The bill's design has some rough edges (the 60-day conversion-fee cutoff could incentivize rotating workers), but the core protections address well-documented problems in the temp staffing model: opaque pay deductions, charge-backs for drug tests, safety gaps, and arbitration clauses.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to eight House committees on the day it was introduced, later pinged to two subcommittees, and no committee ever took it up before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Joseph P. Kennedy III introduced the bill on July 16, 2020, joined by Rep. Emanuel Cleaver II

It was referred the same day to the Education and Labor Committee and seven others: House Administration, Oversight and Reform, Judiciary, Veterans' Affairs, Armed Services, Energy and Commerce, and Natural Resources
In August and September 2020 it was referred to the Subcommittee for Indigenous Peoples (Natural Resources) and the Subcommittee on Oversight and Investigations (Oversight and Reform)
No hearing, markup, report, or floor vote ever occurred; the 116th Congress ended January 3, 2021, with the bill still sitting in committee
Support was limited to the sponsor and 11 Democratic cosponsors, all members of the House majority party, with no Republican support

The bill's core requirements were equal pay for substantially similar work, assignment notices, itemized wage statements, and a ban on forced arbitration, along with safety, registration, and COVID-19 leave provisions

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Temporary staffing agencies and the host employers that hire through them came out ahead: they kept their current pay structures, conversion fees, non-compete practices, and forced arbitration clauses, and faced no new compliance costs. Temp workers gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 sponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and because the bill never reached a vote there is no roll-call record of where the parties stood.

industries.note: Staffing agencies profit on the spread between what host employers pay them and what they pay workers; the bill's equal-pay mandate squeezes that spread, and the bill also ends their conversion fees, non-compete agreements, forced arbitration clauses, and pay deductions for drug tests. It would make them register with the Labor Department and report injury and conversion rates semiannually.

industries.industry: Host employers that staff through agencies (warehousing, manufacturing, hospitals, federal contractors)
industries.note: They would pay higher wages for temp labor and perform job hazard analyses, safety training, and registration verification for every agency contract. The conversion-fee ban cuts their cost of hiring a temp permanently, partially offsetting the increase.
The bill voids predispute arbitration agreements in temp worker employment disputes, removing that stream of arbitration business. Temp workers regain access to federal and state courts instead.
